title: Preferences As The Starting Point

sections.heading: Start From The Ordinary Choice
sections.body: A preference is the course's way of saying that a person can put possible outcomes in an order. The idea starts before strategy, before markets, and before any game table. If a student chooses coffee over tea, or a buyer chooses one apartment over another, the model needs a clear way to record that ordering. The course is not trying to read the person's feelings. It is asking what the person's choices treat as better or worse.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Without preferences, a payoff number has no honest source. A model could still place numbers in a table, but the numbers would float without a reason. Preferences give the model a discipline: first say what outcomes the person ranks above other outcomes, then use utility or payoffs as a compact way to carry that ranking into later problems. This matters because every later result depends on what each player is counted as trying to protect, gain, avoid, or trade away.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to treat preferences as deep psychology or as a claim that people always know exactly what they want. In this course, preferences are a modeling object. They say how the model will compare outcomes inside a chosen problem. That is narrower and more useful. It lets the reader ask whether the rankings are complete enough, whether they create cycles, and whether later payoff numbers really match the story being told.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond The First Lecture
sections.body: Preferences matter in bargaining because the surplus depends on what each side values. They matter in auctions because a bid makes sense only after the bidder has a value for winning. They matter in welfare comparisons because a policy cannot be judged without saying what counts as better for someone. In topology and fixed-point arguments, preferences often enter indirectly through continuous payoff or choice maps; the existence result only means something after the model has said what better means.

applications.body: A policy model must say whose outcomes are being ranked and what tradeoffs count. Otherwise the policy conclusion can hide a value judgment inside a number.
A fixed-point proof may show that a stable choice exists, but preferences and payoffs decide what the map is. Bad rankings make the beautiful proof answer the wrong question.

title: Nash Equilibrium As A No-One-Wants-To-Move Test

sections.heading: Start From A Settled Situation
sections.body: Nash equilibrium begins with a proposed situation, not with a promise that the situation is good. Imagine two firms choosing prices, two drivers choosing routes, or two roommates choosing chores. The question is simple: if everyone else keeps doing what the proposal says, does any one person want to change alone? If the answer is no for every player, the situation passes the Nash test. If even one player wants to move, the proposed story is not stable in this sense.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Strategic stories are easy to tell and hard to trust. Someone can say prices will stay high, both sides will cooperate, or each player will choose a certain action. Nash equilibrium forces that story through a personal incentive check. Each player gets to ask whether a different available action gives a better payoff, holding the others fixed. The concept exists because prediction in a game needs more than a nice story; it needs to survive the pressure of individual deviation.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to hear equilibrium and think fair, peaceful, efficient, or morally right. Nash equilibrium does not say any of that. A traffic jam can be stable because no one driver can improve by switching routes. A bad market outcome can be stable because each firm is already doing its best against the others. The test is narrow: given what everyone else is doing, does one player want to change alone?

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond The Course
sections.body: The idea matters because many systems settle into patterns that are hard to change one person at a time. In politics, a voting rule can hold a poor outcome because each voter faces the same incentives. In networks, people may stay on a platform because others are there. In topology, Nash existence proofs often use fixed-point reasoning: a best-response map points from expected behavior to chosen behavior, and a fixed point is a place where the map sends the behavior back to itself.

applications.body: A platform can be hard to dislodge because each user chooses based on where the other users already are. Stability can come from dependence, not quality.
The fixed point says there is a self-consistent profile under the assumptions. It does not say the profile is efficient, unique, or easy to find.

title: Backward Induction As Solving The Future First

sections.heading: Start From The Last Real Choice
sections.body: Backward induction is the habit of walking to the end of a game tree before judging the beginning. If a later player will eventually choose between accepting and rejecting an offer, start there. Ask what that player will want at that later point. Then carry that answer one step earlier. The early player should not plan around a later threat or promise unless that later action will still make sense when the time comes.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Time changes strategy because words said early can become empty later. A person may threaten to punish, refuse, walk away, or fight, but the model has to ask whether the person will actually want to do that after the earlier choices have already happened. Backward induction exists to remove plans that depend on later actions no one would carry out. It replaces announced resolve with a step-by-step check of later incentives.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to take the first statement in a sequential game at face value. In everyday life, people often make threats that sound strong because they are spoken early. In the model, early speech does not settle credibility. A later decision maker will face a new choice with the past already fixed. Backward induction asks what that person wants then, not what sounded useful before.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Bargaining
sections.body: Backward induction matters in negotiations, entry deterrence, litigation, war threats, hiring processes, and product launches. Any time a choice today is meant to shape a later response, the later response needs its own incentive check. The same idea appears in computer science when an algorithm solves a finite decision tree from the leaves back to the root. It appears in law and policy when a rule must predict how people will respond after enforcement becomes costly.

applications.body: A lawsuit threat affects settlement only if trial would still be worth pursuing later. The later cost of carrying out the threat shapes the earlier bargain.
Finite decision trees can be solved from the end back to the start. The method is the same plain idea: later values guide earlier choices.

title: Infinite Repetition As The Future Pushing Back

sections.heading: Start From A Relationship That Continues
sections.body: An infinitely repeated game is not about literal immortality. It is about a relationship with no known final round inside the model. A firm expects to meet its rival again. A worker expects future reviews. A neighbor expects tomorrow to arrive after today. Because the relationship continues, today's gain from cheating may come with tomorrow's loss from punishment, distrust, or refusal to cooperate.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: One-shot reasoning can make cooperation look impossible because each person sees a short-term temptation. Repetition changes the calculation. If the future is valuable enough and actions are observed well enough, a player may give up a tempting gain today to protect future payoffs. The concept exists because many social and market settings are not one-time encounters. The same people, firms, or institutions keep meeting, and memory can discipline behavior.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to say repeated play automatically creates cooperation. It does not. The future must matter, the bad action must be noticed, and the punishment must be credible. If players are impatient, if monitoring is noisy, or if punishment hurts the punisher too much, cooperation can break. The repeated-game lesson is not optimism. It is a careful comparison between today's temptation and tomorrow's cost.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Firms
sections.body: The idea matters in workplace trust, online reputation, community rules, supply chains, diplomacy, and climate agreements. It explains how present behavior can be shaped by expected future treatment. In biology, repeated interaction can help explain stable cooperation among organisms under the right conditions. In distributed systems, repeated contact and reputation can discourage harmful behavior when no single central enforcer controls every action.

applications.body: A seller may avoid a short-term scam because bad ratings harm future sales. The future is part of the present payoff calculation, and that only works when buyers can observe enough history to punish bad behavior.

Countries may cooperate when future trade, sanctions, monitoring, and reputation make cheating costly enough. The hard part is making those future responses believable, visible, and worth carrying out after the cheating has already happened.

title: Bayesian Games As Strategy With Hidden Facts

sections.heading: Start From Not Knowing Who You Face
sections.body: A Bayesian game begins when a player must choose without knowing some fact that matters. A bidder may not know other bidders' values. A firm may not know a rival's cost. A negotiator may not know whether the other side is patient or desperate. The model calls these hidden facts types. A type is not a personality label. It is the private information that changes payoffs, choices, or beliefs.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Complete-information games pretend that everyone knows the relevant payoff facts. Many important settings do not look like that. If hidden information changes what a player wants, the strategy must say what each possible type would do. Other players then choose using beliefs about which type they may be facing. Bayesian games exist because uncertainty about people is not a footnote; it changes the action that is best.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to average people together too quickly. If half the sellers have high quality and half have low quality, the buyer does not face one average seller in a simple way. The buyer faces uncertainty, and the seller's action may itself give information. A Bayesian model keeps the hidden states separate long enough to ask how each type acts and how others reason from those possible actions.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Auctions
sections.body: Bayesian games matter in insurance, hiring, medical testing, cybersecurity, diplomacy, and any setting where one side knows something the other side must infer. They also matter for topology-based existence work because beliefs and type-contingent strategies enlarge the space in which fixed-point reasoning may be applied. The math can prove a self-consistent plan exists only after the model has clearly named the hidden facts and the belief structure. If those hidden facts are chosen carelessly, the proof may be clean while the lesson is pointed at the wrong uncertainty.

applications.body: An employer does not observe worker fit directly. Schooling, references, interviews, and trial tasks become actions interpreted through beliefs about hidden ability.
A defender may not know the attacker's type, patience, or target. Defensive choices depend on beliefs about hidden motives and costs.

title: Auctions As Rules For Turning Private Values Into Bids

sections.heading: Start From A Simple Sale With Hidden Values
sections.body: An auction is a rule for deciding who gets an object and what they pay when bidders know their own values better than the seller does. The everyday picture is familiar: people want the same item, but each person has a different willingness to pay. The auction rule turns those private values into public bids. The important point is that a bid is not the same thing as a value. It is an action shaped by the payment rule and by competition.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: If a seller knew everyone's value, selling would be easier. With private values, the rule must draw information out through incentives. In a first-price auction, a high bid raises the chance of winning but also raises the price paid if the bidder wins. In a second-price auction, the payment rule changes that tradeoff. Auction theory exists because allocation, payment, belief, and strategic shading have to be studied together.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to think the highest-value bidder simply says the true value in every auction. That can be wrong. A bidder asks what bid gives the best expected surplus, not what bid sounds honest. Different rules change that calculation. Truthful bidding may be a result under special rules, not a natural default. The course makes the rule visible so the reader can see why bidding changes when payment changes.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Selling Objects
sections.body: Auctions matter anywhere a scarce thing must be assigned under private information: spectrum licenses, online ads, school seats, organ exchange priorities, electricity markets, procurement contracts, and platform rankings. The larger lesson is that rules create behavior. A designer who changes the payment rule, reserve price, ranking formula, or information shown to bidders may change both revenue and who receives the object.

applications.body: Governments use bidding rules to buy work from firms with private costs. The rule affects both the winning firm and how much cost information the bids reveal.
Ad slots and rankings are sold through repeated auctions. The design must account for clicks, quality, private value, and strategic bid shading.

title: Signaling As Making Hidden Information Hard To Fake

sections.heading: Start From A Receiver Who Cannot See The Type
sections.body: Signaling starts with a simple problem: one side knows something and the other side cannot see it directly. A worker may know ability, a seller may know quality, and a firm may know whether it is strong or weak. The receiver observes an action, certificate, price, promise, or other sign. The question is not whether the sign looks impressive. The question is whether different hidden types have different incentives to send it.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Information does not move by magic. If a low-quality seller can cheaply copy the high-quality seller's sign, the sign may not separate anyone. Signaling exists because the model must ask whether imitation is profitable. A separating signal works only when each type prefers the action assigned to that type. A pooling signal leaves types together, so the receiver cannot learn much from the observed action.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to treat a signal as proof. A degree, warranty, public promise, expensive building, or high price may mean something, but only after the incentive check. Who would want to send this sign? Who would find it too costly or not worth copying? If the model skips those questions, it can mistake decoration for information. The receiver learns from incentives, not from the sign's appearance alone.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Education
sections.body: Signaling matters in labor markets, product quality, finance, politics, biology, and online identity. It explains why costly actions can carry information and why cheap labels often fail. In biology, displays can signal fitness when weak types cannot easily fake them. In digital systems, verification badges, deposits, history, or costly commitments can help separate reliable participants from unreliable ones, but only when copying remains unattractive.

applications.body: A long warranty can signal confidence only if low-quality sellers expect it to be too costly. The warranty works through incentives, not words.
Badges, deposits, and verified histories can signal reliability when fake accounts cannot cheaply copy the same pattern, or when copying it would remove the gain from pretending online.

title: Common Knowledge As Shared Assurance

sections.heading: Start From A Fact Everyone May Need To Act On
sections.body: Common knowledge is about public assurance, not just information. A fact can be true, and each person can know it, but that may still be too weak for coordination. Each person may wonder whether others know it, whether others know that others know it, and whether everyone is reasoning from the same starting point. Common knowledge is the strong shared state where this ladder keeps going.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Coordination often requires more than private awareness. If a public rule change is announced to everyone at once, people can act knowing that others heard it too. If the same rule is sent privately to each person, the factual content may be identical, but the strategic effect can differ. Common knowledge exists because strategic action can depend on what people believe about other people's beliefs, not only on the first fact.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to say everyone knows and stop there. Everyone knowing can mean each person separately received the fact. It does not always mean each person knows that the others received it, or that this is itself known, and so on. The higher levels sound abstract, but they answer a practical question: can people safely coordinate because they know the fact is shared?

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Classroom Puzzles
sections.body: Common knowledge matters in financial markets, legal announcements, software protocol changes, traffic conventions, political protests, and team work. Public announcements can move behavior because they change the shared reasoning environment. In topology and fixed-point models, common knowledge can affect which game is being solved: the set of strategies, beliefs, and feasible coordination patterns may change when information is public rather than private. The fact itself is only one part of the object; the public status of the fact can change the strategic space.

applications.body: A protocol update works only when participants can treat the rule and its adoption as shared. Private notice may leave coordination risk.
Public news can move prices not only because traders learn the fact, but because they know other traders learned it too.

title: Utility As A Number That Carries A Ranking

sections.heading: Start From Ranking Before Measuring
sections.body: Utility is easy to misunderstand because it uses numbers. The first idea is not that happiness has been measured like weight or height. The first idea is simpler: if a person ranks one outcome above another, the model can sometimes use numbers to carry that ranking. Higher utility means the model treats the outcome as better for that person inside the problem being studied. The number is a tool for comparison, not a claim that the person's inner life has been fully measured.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Game theory needs payoffs because strategic reasoning compares actions. A firm asks whether one price gives more profit than another. A bidder asks whether winning at a price is better than losing. A negotiator asks whether waiting is better than accepting. Utility gives the model a compact way to make those comparisons. Without it, later tools like best response and equilibrium would have nothing to maximize, and the model would only have loose words like wants or likes.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to treat utility as literal pleasure points. In this course, utility is usually a representation of ranked outcomes or payoffs. That difference matters. If the same ranking can be represented by many different number scales, the reader should not over-read the units. The important question is whether the numbers preserve the comparisons the model needs. A utility number is useful when it makes choices checkable without pretending to describe the whole person.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond The First Model
sections.body: Utility matters in economics, political science, law, computer science, public health, and design because models often need to compare tradeoffs. It also matters in topology and fixed-point existence proofs. A best-response map usually comes from players maximizing payoff over a choice set. If the utility function is continuous and the choice set has the right shape, the mathematics may prove a stable point exists. But the meaning of that point still depends on whether utility captured the right tradeoff.

applications.body: A design model must say what users are trading off, such as speed, privacy, cost, or ease. Utility records the tradeoff so choices can be compared.
Existence results often need a well-behaved payoff function. The proof may be formal, but the payoff meaning comes from the modeled ranking.

title: Expected Utility As Choosing Under Risk

sections.heading: Start From Not Knowing Which Outcome Will Happen
sections.body: Expected utility begins when a choice leads to several possible outcomes. A person may buy insurance, enter an auction, invest in a project, or choose a route before knowing the weather. The model cannot pretend the uncertainty is gone. It lists the possible outcomes, assigns probabilities, and averages the utility of those outcomes using those probabilities. The point is not to predict the exact outcome. The point is to compare choices before the uncertainty is resolved.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Many game-theory choices are made before a player knows what kind of opponent, value, cost, or state of the world they face. Expected utility gives the player a way to choose anyway. A bidder compares the chance of winning and the payoff if they win. A firm compares possible demand states. A player in a Bayesian game compares payoffs across possible types. Without expected utility, the course could not connect beliefs to action in a disciplined way.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to average money or outcomes directly without asking what the person values. If a person dislikes risk, a fifty-fifty chance of gaining or losing the same amount may not feel neutral in the model. Expected utility averages utility, not just dollars. Another mistake is to treat the expected value as the thing that will happen. It is a comparison device before the outcome is known, not a promise that the average result will appear.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Lotteries
sections.body: Expected utility matters in insurance, medicine, finance, safety engineering, artificial intelligence, and public decisions under risk. It is also part of the bridge to topology-based equilibrium proofs in games with uncertainty. A player's best response can depend on an expected payoff over unknown states. If those expected payoff functions are well behaved, fixed-point methods can sometimes prove a self-consistent profile exists. The proof rests on the ordinary idea that uncertain outcomes still need a choice rule.

applications.body: A treatment choice may compare possible benefits and harms before anyone knows which patient outcome will occur. Expected utility makes that uncertainty explicit.
An agent choosing under uncertainty needs a rule for trading off possible future states. Expected utility is one plain way to build that rule.

title: Strategic Form Games As A Clean Table Of Mutual Dependence

sections.heading: Start From Choices Made Without Seeing Each Other
sections.body: A strategic form game is the course's compact table for situations where each player's payoff depends on the combination of everyone's choices. The everyday picture is two firms setting prices, two students choosing whether to contribute to a project, or two countries choosing policies without first seeing the other's exact move. The table is not decoration. It is the model's claim about who the players are, what choices they have, and what each outcome gives them.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Game theory needs a way to hold the whole strategic situation in one place. If my payoff depends only on my action, ordinary individual choice may be enough. If my payoff also depends on your action, the model needs a table or function that records the joint effect. Strategic form exists because dependence must be made visible before concepts like dominance, best response, and Nash equilibrium can be applied. The table turns a story into something that can be checked.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to fill in a payoff matrix as if it were obvious. The hardest part is often deciding what belongs in the table. Are players choosing prices, quantities, entry, effort, votes, or messages? Are payoffs money, utility, market share, reputation, or some mix? A strategic form game is only as good as those choices. A neat table can still be wrong if it hides timing, information, or a missing option.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Simple Matrices
sections.body: Strategic form matters in economics, security, traffic routing, platform design, voting, and biology because it provides the first clean picture of mutual dependence. It also matters for topology because many equilibrium existence proofs start with a strategy space and payoff functions defined over action profiles. The fixed point is meaningful only after the strategic form has named the space and payoffs. A poor representation gives a poor map, even if the theorem is correct.

applications.body: A defender's best plan depends on the attacker's plan, and the attacker's payoff depends on the defense. A table makes that dependence inspectable.
Competing traits can be modeled by payoffs that depend on the traits around them. The table records fitness consequences from combinations, not isolated actions.

title: Dominance As Removing A Move With No Good Defense

sections.heading: Start From Comparing Two Choices
sections.body: Dominance starts with a direct comparison. Take one player and compare two possible actions while holding fixed each possible thing the others might do. If one action is never worse and sometimes better, the worse action has no good defense in the model. The player should not need a detailed prediction about others to reject it. The dominated move is bad across the relevant cases.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Before solving a whole game, the course often asks whether some choices can be ruled out immediately. Dominance gives a first cleanup tool. It does not require a full equilibrium story. It only asks whether one action loses to another action across the board. This matters because large games can contain options that distract the reader. Removing a dominated action can reveal the real strategic pressure that remains.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to say an action is dominated because it looks unattractive in one likely case. That is not enough. Dominance is a strong claim about all relevant opponent actions. Another mistake is to treat weak and strict dominance as the same. Weak comparisons can be delicate because deleting a weakly dominated action may change what remains in ways that depend on the order of deletion or on fine details of belief.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Classroom Tables
sections.body: Dominance matters in contract choices, bidding, product strategy, voting rules, and policy design because it identifies options that no reasonable model participant should need. In computer science and operations work, similar pruning ideas remove impossible or inferior branches before a search continues. In topology-heavy equilibrium work, dominance does not replace fixed-point reasoning, but it can simplify the strategy space before asking whether a stable point exists.

applications.body: A planner can discard choices that are never better than another available choice. That reduces clutter before deeper reasoning begins, while still forcing the planner to prove the comparison across all relevant cases.

A voting rule can create dominated voting actions. Finding them shows where the rule asks people to act strategically against their sincere ranking, and where a simpler rule might remove needless manipulation.

title: Rationalizability As Asking What Belief Could Make This Sensible

sections.heading: Start From A Move That Looks Odd
sections.body: Rationalizability begins with a generous everyday question about people choosing under uncertainty. Suppose a player chooses an action that is not immediately ruled out. Could that action be the best response to some reasonable belief about what others will do? If yes, the action has a possible strategic explanation. It may not be the final prediction, and it may not be part of a Nash equilibrium, but it is not foolish inside every possible belief story.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Dominance removes actions that have no defense. Rationalizability studies the actions that survive a belief-based defense. The concept exists because a player's choice can only be judged after saying what they think others might do. A move that looks strange against one opponent action may be sensible against another expected action. Rationalizability keeps belief inside the analysis instead of pretending the analyst already knows the correct forecast.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to treat rationalizable as meaning likely, correct, or socially good. It means the action can be made optimal under some allowable belief. That is a weaker and broader idea than equilibrium. Another mistake is to let any wild belief justify anything. The course still disciplines beliefs through the deletion process and through the assumption that other players are also reasoning about best responses.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Early Solution Concepts
sections.body: Rationalizability matters in legal reasoning, market interpretation, political analysis, and machine learning because observed behavior often has to be interpreted before the analyst knows the actor's beliefs. It also matters near topology because equilibrium can be seen as a stricter self-consistency point, while rationalizability marks a larger set of choices that survive belief-based reasoning. The distinction helps readers understand why fixed-point equilibrium is not the only way to talk about strategic plausibility.

applications.body: An action that seems unreasonable may make sense under one party's belief about the other party. The belief story must still be disciplined.
When agents learn from each other, a move may be sensible under a mistaken but plausible belief. Rationalizability separates that from pure error.

title: Best Response As The Move That Fits A Belief

sections.heading: Start From Freezing The Other Side
sections.body: A best response is the choice that gives a player the highest payoff after the player fixes a belief about what others will do. The idea is ordinary. If a rival sets a high price, one action may be best. If the rival sets a low price, another action may be best. A move is not best in the air. It is best against some expectation, opponent action, or probability story.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Best response is the hinge between individual choice and strategic prediction. Each player is still choosing for themselves, but the choice depends on others. Nash equilibrium is built by putting best responses together. Bayesian Nash uses best responses by type. Repeated games ask whether a continuation plan remains a best response after histories. The concept exists because strategic reasoning needs a local test before it can build a whole-system stability claim.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to call an action best without saying best against what. A price, bid, route, message, or threat can be good under one belief and poor under another. Another mistake is to think a best response must be unique. Sometimes several actions tie. That tie can be important, especially when mixed strategies or equilibrium selection enter. The best-response question is precise because it names the comparison being made.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Game Tables
sections.body: Best responses matter in traffic systems, platform design, pricing, negotiation, cybersecurity, and political campaigns. They are also central to fixed-point reasoning in topology. A best-response correspondence maps what others do into the set of actions a player is willing to choose. An equilibrium is a place where all those response maps fit together. The mathematical theorem may sound abstract, but it is built from the everyday act of asking what choice fits a belief.

applications.body: A driver's best route depends on where other drivers are expected to go. A route can be best at one traffic level and poor at another.
A defender's best response depends on the expected attack path. Changing beliefs about the attacker can change the defense.

title: Mixed Strategies As Randomness With A Strategic Job

sections.heading: Start From Being Too Predictable
sections.body: A mixed strategy means choosing randomly according to a planned probability. The everyday reason is not confusion. It is that predictability can be exploited. A tennis player who always serves left lets the returner prepare. A security team that always patrols the same route invites avoidance. Randomness can be useful when the other side benefits from knowing exactly what you will do.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Some games have no stable prediction in pure actions. If one player picks rock, the other wants paper; if paper, then scissors; if scissors, then rock. The cycle means no fixed pure move survives. Mixed strategies let the model search for stability in probabilities instead. A player may randomize so that the opponent is kept indifferent among certain actions, removing the profitable predictable response.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to treat mixing as a player being careless or unable to decide. In the model, mixing can be deliberate. Another mistake is to think any random probabilities work. Equilibrium mixing has a reason: the probabilities must make opponents willing to play the actions they are supposed to use. The exact numbers carry incentive work. They are not decorative uncertainty pasted onto a deterministic story.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Games Of Chance
sections.body: Mixed strategies matter in sports, inspections, cybersecurity, military planning, pricing, and platform moderation. They also matter for topology because probability mixtures can make strategy sets convex, which is one reason fixed-point existence theorems can apply. The mathematical convenience has a plain meaning: the player is allowed to choose a probability plan rather than only a single action. That expanded space can create a stable point where no pure action profile could.

applications.body: A regulator may randomize inspection times so firms cannot safely hide violations around a known schedule. The randomness creates discipline because the firm cannot make one clean plan around a predictable visit.

Rotating defenses can prevent attackers from exploiting a fixed pattern. The mix must still fit the cost and protection tradeoff, because random movement without purpose can waste effort and leave weak spots exposed.

title: Subgame Perfection As Credibility At Every Later Point

sections.heading: Start From A Plan That Reaches The Future
sections.body: Subgame perfection asks whether an equilibrium plan remains sensible after every later point that could be reached. A plan can be a Nash equilibrium because nobody wants to change at the very start, yet it may rely on a threat that would be foolish later. Subgame perfection tightens the test. It says the strategy must pass the no-deviation logic not only from the beginning, but also inside each proper continuation of the game.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Sequential games need a stronger credibility check than one-shot strategic-form games. A firm may threaten a price war after entry. A negotiator may threaten to reject a future offer. A parent, manager, or government may announce a punishment. The model has to ask whether that future action will be worthwhile once the later moment arrives. Subgame perfection exists because early incentives and later incentives can differ.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to accept any Nash equilibrium in a game tree as a serious prediction. Some Nash equilibria survive only because they contain off-path threats that no one would actually carry out. Subgame perfection rejects those empty threats when the relevant subgame can be evaluated. It does not solve every dynamic information problem, but it teaches the reader to inspect credibility after histories, not just at the root.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Entry Games
sections.body: Subgame perfection matters in bargaining, regulation, litigation, industrial organization, diplomacy, and organizational discipline. It also links to topology and fixed-point thinking through the larger family of equilibrium refinements. Existence of a stable point is not enough when the point is supported by unbelievable future behavior. The refinement asks whether the fixed point has the right internal structure along the time path.

applications.body: A regulator's announced punishment shapes behavior only if the regulator will still want to impose it later. Credibility changes compliance because firms reason about the later enforcement choice, not only the written rule.
A threat can deter action only when carrying it out later is believable. Subgame perfection makes that future check explicit and separates real deterrence from language that sounds strong early.

title: Extensive Form Games As Keeping Time Visible

sections.heading: Start From A Situation That Unfolds
sections.body: An extensive form game is a way to draw a strategic situation as a tree. The everyday reason is simple: sometimes people do not choose all at once. One person moves, another person sees something, a later choice becomes available, and the meaning of an action depends on where the history has gone. A table can hide that timing. A tree keeps the order, the possible histories, and the later decision points visible.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Timing changes incentives. A threat, promise, offer, refusal, or signal can matter only because it happens before or after something else. Extensive form exists because the model needs to know who moves when, what each person sees, and which later choices remain possible. Without that structure, the course could confuse a simultaneous choice with a sequential one and then apply the wrong solution idea.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to think the tree is only a picture of the same information in a prettier form. It is not. A tree can represent facts that a payoff table may hide, such as whether a player observed an earlier move or whether two decision points are indistinguishable to that player. If the information sets or timing are wrong, backward induction and subgame perfection can answer the wrong question.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Game Diagrams
sections.body: Extensive form matters in bargaining, trials, product launches, hiring, military planning, and software protocols because choices happen after histories. It also matters for topology and fixed-point work because the object being solved changes when histories and information sets are included. A fixed point in a strategic form representation may miss credibility problems that only appear once the time path is drawn. That is why the first modeling question is often not how to solve the game, but whether the tree has preserved the real order of action and observation.

applications.body: A protocol is a sequence of actions and observations. Drawing the order helps show which participant knows what before sending the next message.
Settlement, discovery, trial, and appeal happen in order. A legal strategy can only be judged after the later choices and costs are kept visible.

title: Iterated Deletion As Repeatedly Cleaning The Choice Set

sections.heading: Start From Removing One Bad Move
sections.body: Iterated deletion begins with the same everyday thought as dominance: if one choice is never worth taking, remove it. Then the important part happens. Once that move is gone, the game has changed. A choice that was not clearly bad before may become bad after the first cleanup. The process repeats until no more moves can be removed by the rule being used.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Strategic reasoning often works in layers. A player may rule out an action for one opponent, then reason that the opponent will also rule out something else, and so on. Iterated deletion exists because beliefs about other players' rationality can shrink the set of possible behavior step by step. It gives the course a way to show how simple comparisons can have larger consequences after repeated use.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to delete carelessly and then treat the final survivor as unquestionably predicted. The result depends on the deletion rule. Strict dominance is safer than weak dominance. Weak deletion can depend on order and can remove behavior that matters under other beliefs. Iterated deletion is a reasoning tool, not a license to erase choices just because they look unlikely.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Small Games
sections.body: Iterated deletion matters in market entry, voting, auctions, security planning, and algorithmic search because it shows how impossible or indefensible choices can be removed in rounds. In topology-heavy work, deletion can simplify the strategy space before deeper equilibrium reasoning begins, but it must not destroy the assumptions needed for existence or hide the behavior the model was supposed to explain. The method is useful only when every deletion is explained in everyday terms: which choice has lost its defense, and why no belief in the remaining model supports it.

applications.body: A search procedure can prune options, then prune again after the remaining options change. The same caution applies: the pruning rule must be justified.
A firm may first rule out a price, then rule out another price after rivals are expected to rule out their own bad choices.

title: Zero-Sum Games As Pure Conflict

sections.heading: Start From Opposed Payoffs
sections.body: A zero-sum game is a setting where one player's gain is exactly the other player's loss. The everyday picture is not every disagreement. It is a special kind of conflict where the total being divided is fixed inside the model. If I get more, you get less by the same amount. That sharp structure lets the course study protection, exploitation, and security in a cleaner way than general games allow.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Some strategic settings are close enough to pure conflict that cooperation or joint gains are not the main issue. In those settings, the central question is how to avoid being exploited by an opponent with opposite interests. Zero-sum games exist in the course because they give a clear home for minimax reasoning, mixed strategies, and the value of a game. They show what strategic stability looks like when interests are fully opposed.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to call every competitive situation zero-sum. Many markets, negotiations, and political settings have both conflict and shared gains. Two firms may fight over customers but also benefit from market growth. Two countries may compete while still gaining from trade. Calling a mixed-interest setting zero-sum can hide possible agreements, side payments, repeated cooperation, or rule changes that improve outcomes for both sides.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond The Course
sections.body: Zero-sum reasoning matters in games, security, litigation, sports, and adversarial machine learning. It also has a deep mathematical life because minimax theorems and fixed-point ideas are closely related. The topology connection should not obscure the plain meaning: the theorem gives protection in a model where payoffs are exactly opposed. If the world is not actually zero-sum, the clean mathematical result may be answering a narrower question.

applications.body: A defender and attacker can sometimes be modeled with opposed objectives. The zero-sum frame helps ask what defense limits worst-case damage.
One team's gain in a match can be the other team's loss. Mixed and minimax ideas can explain why predictable play is dangerous.

title: Minimax As Protecting Against The Worst Case

sections.heading: Start From A Hostile Response
sections.body: Minimax asks a cautious everyday question: if the other side tries to hurt my payoff, which choice protects me best? The player looks at each possible action, finds the worst outcome the opponent can force against it, and then chooses the action whose worst case is least bad. This is not the same as hoping for the best. It is planning under hostile pressure.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: In zero-sum games, the opponent's gain is your loss, so it makes sense to ask how much damage the opponent can force. Minimax exists because a player may want a security guarantee rather than an optimistic forecast. It gives the course a way to define the value of a zero-sum game and to explain why randomization can be necessary when any fixed action can be exploited.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to use minimax whenever a problem feels risky. Minimax is deliberately pessimistic. It can be too conservative when the opponent is not fully hostile, when probabilities are known, or when both sides can gain together. Another mistake is to ignore the cost of protecting against rare or unrealistic attacks. The method is powerful when worst-case protection is the right goal, not when every tradeoff should be treated as a battle.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Zero-Sum Tables
sections.body: Minimax matters in security, robust engineering, legal strategy, military planning, and algorithm design. It also connects to topology through minimax theorems and fixed-point arguments that prove when protective strategies and game values exist. The everyday meaning remains concrete: the player wants a floor under the outcome. The math is useful only after the analyst has justified why the worst-case frame fits the situation. That fit must be checked in plain language before the protective calculation is treated as a guide for action.

applications.body: A system can be designed to survive the worst stress within a chosen range. The range must be honest or the guarantee misleads.
A party may choose a settlement position by asking what trial outcome the other side could force. That is useful only if trial really is the threat.

title: One-Shot Deviation As A Local Credibility Check

sections.heading: Start From Changing One Move
sections.body: The one-shot deviation principle asks whether a player can gain by changing one action at one decision point while keeping the rest of the plan the same. The everyday idea is local checking. Instead of testing every possible rewritten strategy at once, ask whether any single moment contains a profitable small escape. If no such one-step escape exists under the right conditions, the whole plan passes an important credibility test.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Dynamic strategies can be long and complicated. A plan may say what to do after many histories. Checking every alternative plan directly can be overwhelming. The one-shot deviation principle exists because, in the right class of games, profitable mistakes can be detected through these local deviations. It lets the course inspect sequential rationality without turning every dynamic problem into an unmanageable list of complete strategy rewrites.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to treat the principle as a universal shortcut. It depends on conditions such as the structure of the game and payoff continuity or discounting. Another mistake is to check the intended path only. A strategy also says what happens after histories that might not occur. If an off-path continuation gives someone a profitable one-shot deviation, the proposed plan still has a credibility problem.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Repeated Games
sections.body: The principle matters in contracts, organizational rules, repeated relationships, and policy enforcement because long plans often fail at one concrete future moment. It also links to fixed-point and dynamic programming ideas: local optimality checks can support a global strategic claim when the mathematical conditions are right. The plain lesson is that big promises must survive small later temptations. It is useful because many failures of cooperation are not grand redesigns of the whole plan; they are small moments where one actor quietly wants to do something else.

applications.body: A long contract can fail because one party wants to deviate at one future clause or enforcement moment. Local checks reveal that pressure.
A workplace rule may look stable until a manager has a one-time incentive not to enforce it. The shortcut focuses attention there.

title: Bargaining As Dividing Surplus Under Pressure

sections.heading: Start From Two Sides Who Could Both Gain
sections.body: Bargaining begins when people can create value by reaching agreement, but they disagree about how to divide it. A buyer and seller may both prefer trade to no trade. Workers and firms may both prefer employment to separation. Countries may both prefer peace to conflict. The hard part is not only whether agreement is possible. It is who gets how much, who can wait, and what happens if talks fail.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Ordinary talk about fairness does not settle bargaining. Each side has an outside option, a cost of delay, private information, and a reason to push for a better share. Bargaining theory exists because agreement is strategic. An offer is not only a number; it is a test of what the other side will accept, how patient they are, and what they believe will happen later. Timing and information shape the division.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to say the parties should split the surplus evenly because that sounds reasonable. Equal split may happen in some models, but it is not automatic. A patient side, a side with a better outside option, or a side with private information may get more. Another mistake is to ignore delay. Waiting can be a bargaining weapon, but it can also destroy value.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Negotiation Examples
sections.body: Bargaining matters in wages, mergers, settlements, household decisions, international agreements, and platform contracts. It also connects to topology because some bargaining solutions are existence or fixed-point claims about feasible sets and preferences. The mathematical object must still answer a plain question: which agreements are possible, which disagreement outcome matters, and why would each side accept the proposed division? The same structure appears whenever people can jointly gain but must decide who captures the gain and who bears the cost of delay.

applications.body: Wages depend not only on productivity but also on outside options, patience, replacement costs, and what each side believes the other will accept.
A settlement divides the expected surplus from avoiding trial. Delay, risk, and private information can prevent agreement even when settlement would save costs.

title: Finitely Repeated Games As The Last Round Pushing Backward

sections.heading: Start From A Relationship With A Known End
sections.body: A finitely repeated game is a repeated relationship with a known last round. People meet more than once, but everyone knows when the interaction stops. That known ending changes the logic. In the last round, there is no future punishment left inside the model. If cooperation requires fear of later punishment, the last round may unravel first, and earlier rounds can be affected by that future endpoint.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Repeated play can support cooperation when the future matters, but a known final period weakens that force. The concept exists because the course needs to separate ongoing relationships from relationships with a fixed end. A worker near final review, a firm near the last contract, or a player near the final round may face different incentives. The end of the relationship can reach backward into present behavior.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to assume that repetition always helps cooperation. If everyone knows the final round and the stage game has a unique noncooperative equilibrium, backward reasoning can make cooperation unravel. Another mistake is to apply the stark unraveling result without checking the assumptions. Reputation, incomplete information, social norms, outside enforcement, or multiple equilibria can change the conclusion. The result is strongest when the endpoint is truly known, behavior is observed, and no outside relationship carries consequences beyond the modeled last round.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Repeated Prisoners Dilemmas
sections.body: Finitely repeated games matter in employment contracts, supply relationships, political terms, school projects, and temporary alliances. They also clarify the boundary of fixed-point existence thinking. A stable plan in a repeated game must respect the known time horizon. The topology of the strategy space cannot make future punishment meaningful after the modeled future has ended. The lesson is practical: when a relationship has a visible end, the analyst should ask which incentives survive the end and which incentives vanish.

applications.body: A politician facing a final term may have weaker future electoral discipline. The known endpoint changes present incentives.
A group with a final deadline may cooperate early but slack near the end if no future response remains inside the relationship.

title: Folk Theorem As Many Outcomes When The Future Matters

sections.heading: Start From Future Punishment Supporting Today
sections.body: The folk theorem is a family of results about repeated games. The everyday idea is that patient players can sometimes sustain many different outcomes because future punishment makes today's temptation unattractive. If cheating now brings a short gain but triggers a long future loss, cooperation or other disciplined behavior may be stable. The theorem explains why repeated interaction can support much more than the one-shot game suggests.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Infinitely repeated games often have many possible equilibria. The course needs a way to say how large that set can be and what makes it possible. The folk theorem exists because future incentives can turn many feasible and individually acceptable payoff patterns into self-enforcing outcomes. It is not one prediction. It is a warning that repetition can create a wide menu of stable arrangements.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to treat the folk theorem as saying cooperation will happen. It does not. It says many outcomes can be sustained under strong enough patience and credible punishment conditions. That abundance can make prediction harder, not easier. Another mistake is to ignore monitoring. If players cannot observe cheating well enough, they may punish the wrong person or fail to punish the right one.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond The Theorem Statement
sections.body: The folk theorem matters in cartels, workplace norms, diplomacy, informal credit, online communities, and repeated platform behavior. It also has a mathematical side involving feasible payoff sets, discounting, and equilibrium construction. The topology or geometry of payoff sets can be elegant, but the plain lesson is practical: when the future is powerful, many behavior patterns may be stable, so extra institutional detail is needed for sharp prediction. It pushes the reader to ask which punishment, norm, or selection story chooses one outcome from the many that the repeated game can support.

applications.body: A group can sustain many informal rules when future inclusion matters. The rule survives only if members observe and respond to violations.
Repeated contact can support restraint, retaliation, or cooperation. The theorem warns that several stable patterns may fit the same basic incentives.

title: Implicit Cartels As Cooperation Without A Spoken Deal

sections.heading: Start From Firms That Keep Meeting
sections.body: An implicit cartel is a situation where firms act as if they are restraining competition even without an explicit agreement. The everyday picture is repeated rivalry. Each firm may want to cut price today and steal customers, but it also knows rivals can respond tomorrow. High prices can survive when the future loss from retaliation outweighs the short-term gain from undercutting.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Competition policy cannot look only for written contracts or secret meetings. Firms may coordinate through repeated market behavior, public price changes, or mutual understanding of punishment. The concept exists because repeated-game incentives can make collusion self-enforcing without a formal cartel. The model asks whether each firm would rather keep the high-price pattern than cheat and face future punishment.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to treat every high price as proof of an implicit cartel. High prices can also come from costs, product quality, capacity limits, search frictions, or lawful differentiation. Another mistake is to ignore credibility. If firms cannot observe cheating or cannot punish profitably, the cartel-like outcome may not be stable. The repeated-game story needs evidence, not only suspicion.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Antitrust
sections.body: Implicit cartel reasoning matters in platform markets, procurement, labor markets, and any repeated setting where rivals watch one another. It also shows why topology or fixed-point existence is not enough by itself. A stable collusive pattern may exist mathematically, but policy needs to know whether monitoring, punishment, and market institutions make that pattern realistic and harmful. The plain-language question is whether future rivalry supplies enough discipline to replace an explicit contract. This makes the concept useful but also dangerous: it can explain quiet coordination, yet it must be tied to market facts before accusing firms of collusion.

applications.body: Regulators must separate lawful parallel behavior from repeated-game coordination. Evidence about monitoring and punishment is central. The review should ask who observes price cuts, how quickly rivals respond, and whether punishment would be profitable.
Repeated bidders may learn to rotate wins or avoid aggressive bids. The pattern can persist without a written agreement.

title: Imperfect Competition As Firms With Market Power And Rivals

sections.heading: Start From The Middle Between Monopoly And Perfect Competition
sections.body: Imperfect competition is the middle case where a firm has some power over price or quantity, but it is not alone. A monopoly can act without a strategic rival inside the market. A perfectly competitive firm is too small to move the price. Imperfect competition is messier and more common: each firm matters, and each firm must think about how rivals respond.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: The course needs imperfect competition because real markets often have a few important firms. Profit depends on demand, cost, and rival behavior. A firm's best quantity in Cournot competition differs from its best price in Bertrand competition because the strategic variable changes. The concept exists to show that market power is not a single story. The model must say what firms choose and how those choices affect one another.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to say competition means price equals cost or monopoly means one firm, then force every market into those extremes. Many markets sit between them. Another mistake is to treat Cournot and Bertrand as interchangeable labels. Quantity competition and price competition can give different predictions. The representation is not cosmetic; it carries the strategic pressure. The analyst has to defend the market model before trusting the prediction that comes out of it.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Industrial Organization
sections.body: Imperfect competition matters in tech platforms, hospitals, airlines, retail, labor markets, and energy markets. It also links to topology because equilibrium existence often depends on firms' strategy sets and payoff functions. The mathematical proof of a stable profile is useful only after the analyst has defended whether firms choose prices, quantities, capacity, quality, or some other strategic variable. That choice is a first-principles decision, not a technical afterthought, because it decides what rivalry means in the model.

applications.body: A platform may choose fees, ranking rules, or access terms while rivals do the same. Market power and strategic dependence operate together.
Hospitals or insurers may have local market power while still facing rivals. Policy analysis must model both power and response.

title: Types And Beliefs As Naming Hidden Facts And Guesses

sections.heading: Start From What One Side Cannot See
sections.body: Types and beliefs separate two everyday things that are often mixed together. A type is the hidden fact: a bidder's value, a seller's quality, a worker's ability, or a firm's cost. A belief is someone else's probability story about that hidden fact. The distinction matters because truth and guess are not the same. The model needs both the hidden state and the way players reason about it.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Private information changes strategy. If a player knows their own type, their action may depend on it. If others do not know that type, they must act using beliefs. Types and beliefs exist because the course needs a clean place to store hidden information and a clean way to represent uncertainty about it. Without them, Bayesian games, signaling, screening, and perfect Bayesian equilibrium would collapse into vague talk about not knowing.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to treat type as a personality category or belief as a casual opinion. In the model, a type is the payoff-relevant private information, and a belief is a probability distribution used for choice. Another mistake is to choose types after seeing the desired answer. If the type space is badly chosen, the equilibrium may be internally consistent but explain the wrong hidden fact.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Economics
sections.body: Types and beliefs matter in medicine, hiring, insurance, cybersecurity, law, and machine learning because decisions often turn on hidden states. They also matter in topology-based equilibrium proofs because beliefs can be part of the strategy space or state space. A fixed point over beliefs and actions is only meaningful when the type model honestly captures the uncertainty people face. The reader should always ask whether the hidden fact is real, payoff-relevant, and visible to the person whose type the model names.

applications.body: A doctor may not know a patient's hidden condition and must use test results as evidence. The condition is like a type; the diagnosis is a belief.
A defender may not know whether an observed actor is a casual user, bot, or attacker. The response depends on beliefs about that hidden type.

title: Bayesian Nash Equilibrium As Stability For Each Type

sections.heading: Start From Each Type Having A Plan
sections.body: Bayesian Nash equilibrium extends the no-one-wants-to-move idea to games with hidden information. A strategy is no longer just one action for a player. It can be a plan for each possible type of that player. A high-value bidder may bid differently from a low-value bidder. A low-cost firm may choose differently from a high-cost firm. The equilibrium asks whether each type is best responding given beliefs about everyone else.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Nash equilibrium assumes the relevant payoff facts are known. Bayesian games do not. Bayesian Nash exists because every hidden type needs its own incentive check. The low type must not want to switch from its plan, and the high type must not want to switch from its plan, given beliefs and other players' type-contingent strategies. Stability must hold before private information is fully revealed.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to check only the player as a whole. In a Bayesian setting, each type is a different decision problem. Another mistake is to forget beliefs. A plan can look strange until the reader asks what the type thinks others are likely to be. Bayesian Nash equilibrium is not just Nash with extra vocabulary; it changes what a strategy is and where best-response checks happen.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Auctions
sections.body: Bayesian Nash matters in auctions, insurance, hiring, procurement, security, and any setting where hidden facts shape action. It also connects to fixed-point reasoning because equilibrium may be proven over spaces of type-contingent strategies. The topology can show a self-consistent plan exists, but the plain question remains: is every type willing to follow its assigned plan under its beliefs? This makes the concept useful far beyond bidding: any hidden-information setting needs a plan that each possible type can defend.

applications.body: Low-cost and high-cost firms may bid differently. Bayesian Nash checks whether each cost type is willing to follow its bidding rule.
Different worker types may choose different signals or applications. Employers respond using beliefs about which type they face.

title: Screening And Adverse Selection As Rules Changing Who Shows Up

sections.heading: Start From Hidden Quality Or Cost
sections.body: Screening and adverse selection begin when one side knows something important that the other side cannot see. A seller knows product quality, a worker knows effort cost, an insured person knows risk, or a bargaining partner knows value. The uninformed side sets a price, contract, or rule. That rule does not just divide surplus. It changes which hidden types choose to participate.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Trade can fail even when trade would create value under full information. If a buyer offers an average price for used goods, high-quality sellers may leave, lowering the average quality of those who remain. Insurance prices can push low-risk people out, leaving a riskier pool. The concept exists because selection changes the group being analyzed. The average after people respond is not the same as the average before the rule.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to say there are gains from trade, so agreement should happen. Hidden information can block that simple logic. Another mistake is to ignore participation. A contract that looks profitable against the whole population may attract only the types that make it unprofitable. Screening tries to design choices that separate types, but it must give each type a reason to choose the intended option.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Market Examples
sections.body: Screening and adverse selection matter in insurance, credit, hiring, college admissions, platform trust, medical markets, and regulation. They also connect to topology and equilibrium because participation rules can change the feasible set and the belief distribution. A stable outcome may exist, but the important question is which types remain in the market and which valuable trades disappear. The everyday warning is that the rule does not meet a fixed crowd; it helps create the crowd it will later face. This is why participation is part of the model rather than an afterthought; the people who accept the rule are selected by the rule itself.

applications.body: A high premium may drive low-risk people away, leaving a riskier pool. The price changes who buys the contract.
A test or credential can screen applicants, but only if different worker types face different costs or benefits from completing it.

title: Revenue Equivalence As Same Expected Money Under Strong Conditions

sections.heading: Start From Different Auction Rules
sections.body: Revenue equivalence asks how different auction formats can sometimes give the seller the same expected revenue. A first-price auction and a second-price auction look different. In one, the winner pays their own bid. In the other, the winner pays someone else's bid. The surprise is that under specific assumptions, bidders adjust their strategies so expected payments line up.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: The theorem exists because surface rules do not tell the whole story. Bidders respond to rules. A first-price bidder shades the bid because paying the bid is costly. A second-price bidder may have a reason to bid truthfully under the standard assumptions. Revenue equivalence teaches the reader to compare allocation probabilities and expected payments, not just auction names. The same revenue can arise from different behavior.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to treat revenue equivalence as saying auction design does not matter. It says equivalence can hold when the assumptions line up. Change risk aversion, reserve prices, common values, bidder symmetry, entry, or the allocation rule, and the conclusion can fail. The theorem is useful partly because it tells the analyst which assumptions are doing the work. Those failures are not embarrassing exceptions; they show which economic force the simple theorem intentionally set aside.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Auction Class
sections.body: Revenue equivalence matters in procurement, spectrum sales, online platforms, and mechanism design because it separates rule labels from incentive effects. It also has a mathematical lesson: two different-looking mechanisms can induce the same expected transfer when their payoff objects match. The topology or calculus behind the result is less important than the plain warning to inspect assumptions before comparing institutions. The result is a discipline for comparison: before saying one rule raises more money, ask whether bidders adjust in a way that offsets the surface difference.

applications.body: A government comparing auction formats must ask whether the theorem's assumptions fit the bidders and object. If not, revenue may differ sharply.
Online platforms often change reserve prices, quality scores, and entry rules. Those details can break equivalence even when formats look familiar.

title: Ad Auctions As Selling Attention Through Rules

sections.heading: Start From Ranked Attention
sections.body: Ad auctions sell attention, not a simple object on a shelf. A search page or feed has positions, and those positions differ in click probability and value. Advertisers have private values for clicks or conversions. The platform must decide who appears where and what each advertiser pays. The bid is only one piece of the story; quality, relevance, position, and user behavior may also matter.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Standard auction theory is not enough for online ads because the object is ranked, repeated, and measured through user response. A higher slot may get more clicks. A low-quality ad may harm users. A platform may use quality scores or generalized second-price rules to balance revenue and relevance. Ad auctions exist in the course because they show how clean auction ideas must be adapted when institutions become engineered systems.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to think the highest bid simply buys the best slot. Many platforms rank by bid times quality or use other scoring rules. Another mistake is to confuse price per click with value per click. Advertisers bid strategically based on expected profit, not just exposure. The platform's formula changes behavior, so the rule must be part of the model.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Advertising
sections.body: Ad auctions matter for search, social media, app stores, creator markets, and any ranking system that allocates scarce visibility. They also connect to topology and equilibrium because advertisers repeatedly choose bids in response to a rule and to each other. A stable bidding profile may exist, but the policy question also asks whether the rule serves users, advertisers, and platform incentives in the intended way. That is why ad auctions sit between economics and product design: the rule changes money, information, and the quality of what users see. A good explanation must therefore follow the chain from bid to rank to click to payment, rather than stopping at the auction label.

applications.body: A search engine allocates visible slots by combining bids, predicted clicks, and quality. The design affects advertiser behavior and user experience.
Sponsored placement can work like an ad auction. The ranking rule decides whose attention is sold and how strategic bids change visibility.

title: Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium As Beliefs And Actions Moving Together

sections.heading: Start From A Dynamic Game With Hidden Information
sections.body: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium is used when a game has both time and private information. A player observes an action, but not always the hidden type that produced it. The player must form a belief, then choose a response. The sender or earlier mover must also want to act as planned given how later players will interpret the action. Beliefs and actions discipline each other.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Bayesian Nash handles hidden information in a more static way, and subgame perfection handles credibility in games with clearer information. Perfect Bayesian equilibrium exists because signaling and other dynamic information games need both checks at once. Players must act optimally after histories, and beliefs should be updated by Bayes' rule when the observed behavior makes that possible. A proposed story must explain both what people do and what they infer.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to state strategies without beliefs, or beliefs without checking whether actions are optimal under them. In a signaling game, a receiver's response depends on what the signal says about type. But the signal says something only if the sender types actually want to send different signals. PBE forces that loop to close. It does not let the analyst freely assign beliefs just to save a favorite outcome.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Signaling Models
sections.body: Perfect Bayesian equilibrium matters in bargaining with incomplete information, reputation, education, warranties, regulation, and diplomacy. It also relates to fixed-point thinking because strategies and beliefs form a coupled object. The mathematical challenge is to find a self-consistent pair, but the everyday meaning is clear: after people observe behavior, their guesses and future actions must still make sense. This is why the concept is demanding: it does not let the story choose convenient beliefs after the fact.

applications.body: A firm may act tough early so others believe it is a tough type. PBE asks whether that action and belief are mutually supported.
A warranty can change beliefs about product quality only if different seller types have different incentives to offer it.

title: Cheap Talk As Words That Need Incentive Support

sections.heading: Start From A Message That Costs Nothing
sections.body: Cheap talk is communication that is costless and nonbinding. A person can say a state is good, a project is safe, a product is high quality, or a policy will work. The message itself does not force truth. The receiver must ask why the sender would want to say that message in different states. Words can still matter, but they need incentive support.

sections.heading: Why The Idea Has To Exist
sections.body: Many strategic settings include advice, promises, recommendations, labels, and forecasts. Ignoring speech misses an important part of behavior, but trusting speech automatically is also wrong. Cheap talk exists because communication can change beliefs when sender and receiver incentives are aligned enough. When incentives are opposed, every type may want to send the same flattering message, and the message may reveal little.

sections.heading: The Common Mistake
sections.body: The mistake is to say cheap means useless. Costless talk can matter when the sender and receiver partly want the same action. Another mistake is to treat a message as evidence without checking incentives. If every sender type benefits when the receiver believes the best possible story, then the message may pool all types together. The model asks what each type would actually want to say.

sections.heading: Why It Matters Beyond Simple Sender Receiver Games
sections.body: Cheap talk matters in management, medical advice, financial forecasts, politics, platform reviews, diplomacy, and everyday negotiation. It also connects to topology and equilibrium because possible communication rules can be part of a strategic fixed point: messages, beliefs, and actions must fit together. The plain lesson is that language changes outcomes only when the incentive structure lets listeners learn something useful. The model therefore treats speech as an action inside incentives, not as a separate layer floating above the game.

applications.body: A manager's advice can guide a worker when both want the project to succeed. It becomes less informative when their goals diverge.

Campaign messages are cheap talk unless voters can connect them to incentives, records, constraints, or costly commitments. Voters need reasons to believe the message, such as records, constraints, shared interests, or costly follow-through.
